newsitem.title: UK: UK union asks firms to negotiate on social chapter.
newsitem.headline: UK union asks firms to negotiate on social chapter.

text.p: Britain's Trades Union Congress (TUC) has written to the country's top 300 companies, inviting them to negotiate on measures to be introduced under the European Union's social chapter.

In the letter, published by the union umbrella body on Thursday, TUC general secretary John Monks said the unions wanted "to put adversarial industrial relations behind us" and seek a consensus on social change.
"While the TUC does favour minimum workplace standards...we are not in favour of rigid rules that do not take account of the specifics of the British workplace," he wrote.
The Social Chapter of the EU's Maastricht Treaty provides a framework for introducing minimum workplace standards across Europe.

Monks noted that only two measures had so far been introduced under the Chapter -- European Works Councils and unpaid parental leave -- and both had been brought in after talks between unions and employers.

"It is absurd to claim that the Social Chapter will cost jobs," he said, adding that a recent TUC survey of Britain's top 50 companies had found that they were generally exceeding the requirements of both the social chapter and the working time directive.
The latter, fiercely opposed by the current Conservative government, like the Social Chapter, contains rules on working hours and holidays.
The government failed last year in a bid to the European Court of Justice to have British firms exempted from this EU health and safety directive.

British unions are closely linked to the Labour Party, which is widely expected to win the May 1 election. Labour leader Tony Blair has promised the unions no favours, although he is committed to adopting the Social Chapter.
Monks has over the past few years given the union movement a more responsible face and tried to advance the cause of employees through negotiation.
"An approach based on what the EU calls social partnership could be helpful," he said in his letter to the top companies.

"Measures agreed under the European Social Chapter do allow for flexibility in their implementation under national law. Just as the framework for these national agreements is negotiated at European level between employers and unions, it makes good sense to do the same in Britain," he added.
